BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: An upper level ridge centered to our east will amplify through late week. The building ridge and increased southerly flow will increase temperatures a few more degrees.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A pair of weak systems will bring light rain showers to the area, one today north of a line from Baker City to McCall, and another generally north of Boise Monday night.
- Above normal temperatures continue through the week. Record highs are possible, especially mid week.
- A cooler, wetter pattern is likely to develop next weekend or early the following week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A trough will move across Washington today while a ridge of high pressure remains anchored across the Southwest and extends across the Plains. The trough will bring isolated showers to northeast Oregon and west-central Idaho today, generally north of a Baker City OR to McCall ID line, while the ridge keeps conditions dry elsewhere. Similarly, temperatures across the north will be a few degrees cooler while across the south highs will be similar to Saturday, around 10 degrees above normal. However, the system will bring mostly cloudy skies and breezy winds to all areas. Winds will be strongest this morning from the southeast with gusts 15-25 mph, gradually subsiding this afternoon.

The ridge will remain in place through Tuesday, but another system moving through the Pacific Northwest will clip the area Monday night. This will once again bring a chance of showers to the north while southern areas only see high clouds. This system will be slightly deeper than the system today, resulting in a 20-50% chance of showers generally north of Boise, except a 50-80% chance across the west-central Idaho mountains. Snow levels will remain above 7000 feet limiting light snow accumulation to the peaks, with light rain amounts at lower elevations. Conditions will dry out Tuesday with decreasing clouds. Winds will become a bit breezy ahead of this system on Monday, then decrease on Tuesday as the system moves east. Highs will remain 10-15 degrees above normal Monday and Tuesday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: An upper level ridge centered to our east will amplify through late week. The building ridge and increased southerly flow will increase temperatures a few more degrees. This will place max temperatures near daily record highs, and lower valleys are forecast to reach the mid to upper 60s and may approach 70F. A deep upper level trough approaching the coast will split mid week, with the southern portion closing off and diving south to southern California. The northern portion is favored to remain off the coast initially, continuing mild and dry conditions. However, some global ensemble members bring it inland enough for a 10-30% chance of showers, with the highest chance across the north and the mountains. Confidence is higher that the trough will progress inland by Sunday or early next week, bringing the potential for widespread precipitation and cooler temperatures. The amplified pattern will bring breezy south to southeasterly winds mid week, increasing late week into the weekend as the trough approaches.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: For Thursday into the weekend, an upper level ridge builds over the area, bringing temps back to 10-15 degrees above normal for the plains on Friday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above normal temperatures and dry conditions are expected for at least the next seven days.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Upper level high pressure will further build into the area Sunday and Monday, keeping well-above normal temperatures and dry conditions across the area. Mostly sunny to partly cloudy skies are forecast for the next two days, with highs approaching 70 degrees each afternoon for portions of the plains.

On Tuesday, the flow aloft becomes more zonal, and potentially even a little northwesterly. A shortwave trough is forecast to approach the area from the northwest, bringing slightly cooler temperatures aloft and increased cloud cover for Tuesday afternoon. This will allow temperatures to drop a few degrees for Tuesday afternoon in the higher terrain and portions of the plains. A cold front is forecast to move through sometime mid Tuesday into early Wednesday. Models vary pretty significantly with the positioning and strength of the shortwave and therefore the strength of the cold front. The GFS wants to bring the shortwave further south into the area, with a much stronger cold front. It also brings the 700mb jet over the northeast plains, putting breezy winds across the area late Tuesday into Wednesday. This solution would allow for low end rain chances in the higher terrain, warmer temperatures across the northern plains on Tuesday from strong downsloping, and cooler temperatures Wednesday. However, other models have a less potent shortwave staying more to our northeast. With this solution precipitation chances would remain near zero, surface winds would be much lighter, and temperatures would drop slightly for the middle of the week, but not as significantly as the other scenario.

For Thursday into the weekend, an upper level ridge builds over the area, bringing temps back to 10-15 degrees above normal for the plains on Friday. Looking at ensembles, there is not a single member of the most recent GFS and ECMWF runs that have even a trace of rain for Denver over the next 7 days, so confidence is high in conditions staying dry for the plains (unfortunately).

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Behind the departing clipper system, ensembles are in excellent agreement showing a highly amplified ridge building in over the Rockies Thursday into the following weekend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Near to or just above average temperatures and dry conditions are expected to continue into mid-week.
- Breezier winds return today into Monday; however, fire weather conditions are not anticipated at this time.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Rinse and repeat, another pleasant day is on tap with mainly sunny skies and mild temperatures as we sit under a bubble of high pressure bringing us benign weather. So, expect high temperatures this afternoon to top out slightly above average for this time of year. Locations along and west of the Laramie Range will see highs in the mid 50s to low 60s while many locations along and east of the I-25 corridor will see highs soar into the low 60s to mid/upper 60s. Warmest across far eastern Wyoming and in the Nebraska Panhandle where a few locations may see highs topping out around 70. Lows Sunday night will mainly bottom out into the upper 30s to low 40s, a few valleys west of I-25 may see lows tank into the low 30s. Switching gears a bit, today compared to previous days will be the noticeably different in regards to winds, it will be much breezier, especially in the wind prones. The mid-level flow will ramp up with 700 mb westerly winds increasing into the 35 to 40 knot range. With ample subsidence, negative Omega (GFS), these winds will make it down to the surface, especially along the higher peaks of the Laramie Range. This is confirmed by our in-house guidance where the height gradient between Craig and Casper reaches a max around 45 meters today into Monday. This translates to wind gusts at the surface on the order of up to 45 mph, just below High Wind criteria. As we head into Monday, the ridge aloft over the forecast area will flatten out as the upper level flow becomes zonal. In this, a weak surface front will dive south to southwest into the Laramie Range. This will keep winds gusty from the Laramie Range and points west. With the ridge being the dominant feature, we will continue to see above average temperatures Monday along with continued benign conditions. Therefore, highs on Monday west of the Laramie Range look to top out in the mid 50s to low 60s. While highs along and east of the I-25 corridor will soar into the mid to upper 60s. Lows Monday night will bottom out generally in the mid 30s.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Warm and dry weather looks to continue for the forseeable future. A weak and moisture starved clipper system will traverse near the area on Tuesday into Wednesday. A few sprinkles or flurries will be possible, but only a small minority of ensemble members support any precipitation whatsoever for the region. Expect this to knock 700-mb temperatures down to the 0 to +2C range, while pulling the surface trough well east of the Laramie Range. This will allow breezy conditions to spread into the High Plains. Temperatures are expected to remain above seasonal averages, but with the cool down we should be a little closer to normal (perhaps 5 to 8F above average). While most will be breezy, high winds are fairly unlikely. In-house guidance shows probabilities around 20 to 30% for the typical wind prone areas.

Behind the departing clipper system, ensembles are in excellent agreement showing a highly amplified ridge building in over the Rockies Thursday into the following weekend. This feature will block or deflect any incoming storm systems, and push temperatures well above average once again. Since we'll be on the periphery of this ridge, temperature expectations are not too extreme. 700-mb temperatures around +4 to +6C are currently shown in the NAEFS mean, which is near the climatological 90th percentile. This isn't quite warm enough to support record highs, but expect temperatures at the surface to range a good 10 to 15F above seasonal norms. The strong ridge will likely also keep winds fairly light during this period.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: The string of mostly sunny and dry days will stretch well into next week as we continue to dry out from an extraordinary wet and cool end of October. The 08/00Z H500 hand analysis map is showing a tilted Rex block over the West/Southwest.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Mostly clear conditions and near to above normal temperatures will continue well into next week.
- Some patchy overnight fog is possible in the favored valleys especially over eastern Utah where soils remain highly saturated.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The string of mostly sunny and dry days will stretch well into next week as we continue to dry out from an extraordinary wet and cool end of October. The 08/00Z H500 hand analysis map is showing a tilted Rex block over the West/Southwest. The blocking high in this pattern has forced the jet and any associated moisture well to our North. This ridge will hold strong as it elongates across the Intermountain West to the Central High Plains through early next week. Temperatures will remain on the high side of normal in most areas through this time. The desert valleys...either due to soggy soils or strong low level inversions...will run closer to normal. The inversions and trapped moisture in the planetary boundary layer could lead to some fog in some of the valleys...but this is a low confidence forecast. A northern stream wave dropping out of the Northern Rockies to the High Plains by mid week will force the ridge back to the West. This will have minimal impact to our sensible weather and persistence to our warm and dry forecast continues. The ridge looks to be forced once again back into the Rockies by the end of the week as a closed low replaces it back to the West over eastern Pacific.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Based on the longer range guidance, the better chance of seeing precip returning to the region will be late next week. \/Hodanish

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry conditions with above seasonal temps during this forecast period for this time of the year.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Today and Tonight...SW-NE mid level ridge axis will be over the region through the next 24 hours. This will keep mainly clear skies over the region. Temps will range from 4 to 6F above normal for this time of the year, with max temps in the ~M60s plains and ~M50s valleys.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Predominantly dry. Temps overall will be in the 60s plains and 50s valley. Monday should be the warmest day of the week with some L70s over the plains and upper 50s in the valleys. Coolest day is expected to be Wed as a modest, albeit dry, mid level short wave drops southeast over the region. Max temps over the plains are expected to fall into the 60-65F range while mid 50s are expected over the valleys. We will likely see breezy conditions on this day.

If we see any precip during this period, it will likely be Sunday as a leading short wave in advance of a large Pacific trough moves into the region. However, models do not unanimously agree with this as the Euro is slower while the GFS is quicker with the system. DESI statistical guidance keeps it dry over the region.
Based on the longer range guidance, the better chance of seeing precip returning to the region will be late next week. \/Hodanish

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Ensembles have diverged in the progression of the aforementioned trough as we head into next weekend, with around 20% of members supportive of a shortwave ejecting off the parent trough and bringing increased chances for precipitation as early as Saturday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Patchy fog is expected to develop tonight in prone areas such as the Cache Valley.
- Conditions remain dry and mild areawide through a majority of the week, with the next chance for precipitation arriving next weekend.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: With clear skies in place across the region, patchy fog is expected to develop in fog prone areas such as the Cache Valley. Fog will dissipate through Sunday morning, with additional chances for fog development overnight Sunday decreasing due to increasing cloud cover across northern Utah.

Quiescent conditions with a gradual warming trend prevails into early this upcoming week as longwave ridging remains the dominant feature across the region. Warming aloft through this period will allow valley inversions to strengthen, resulting in hazy skies. A weak shortwave trough is slated to traverse northern Utah on Tuesday, ushering in slightly cooler air aloft, which may assist in mixing out some valley haze. Following the departure of this weak wave, high pressure re-amplifies across the region in response to a trough deepening off the west coast.

Ensembles have diverged in the progression of the aforementioned trough as we head into next weekend, with around 20% of members supportive of a shortwave ejecting off the parent trough and bringing increased chances for precipitation as early as Saturday. The remainder of models eject this energy too far south for any meaningful precipitation outside of slight chances across southern Utah. Regardless, the pattern looks to remain more progressive, though the exact storm track is uncertain at this point.

2660.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Although avalanche conditions are generally safe, you'll still want to steer clear of stiff wind-drifted pockets of snow in the alpine. You are more likely to trigger an avalanche in wind-drifted snow on slopes that face the north half of the compass.
Continued weakening (faceting) of the upper snowpack will start to lead to small sluffs.

2747.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: Most slopes hold too little snow to produce an avalanche. At high elevations, steer around areas of firm, drifted snow if you find them below ridges or in gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Most slopes are generally safe for travel. If you see evidence of recent wind-drifting on a steep slope or find a thicker slab at higher elevations on the north half of the compass, consider avoiding that terrain. Stiffer pockets of wind-drifted snow that could produce a small slide are common, like just below ridgelines and along gully walls. Most slopes near and below treeline hold too little snow to produce an avalanche.
